newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai T-bill repo rates end down, spots up.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai T-bill repo rates end down, spots up.

text.p: Contracts on the treasury bill repurchase market in Shanghai closed mixed on Friday on a lack of market-moving news ahead of the weekend, traders said.
The annual rate for the shortest three-day contract hit a record low of 1.22 percent, down from Thursday's 3.58 percent, due to dull trading, traders said.

But the rate for the most actively traded seven-day contract rose to 6.95 percent from 5.50 percent, with some investors borrowing to prepare for a new domestic A share issue on the Shenzhen stock exchange next Monday, traders said.
Total turnover of the six-contract market fell sharply to 1.14 million lots from 1.81 million lots.
One lot is 1,000 yuan face value of treasury bills.
Traders said most institutions traded less ahead of the weekend with no market-moving news around the corner.
"The three-day contract set a record low due to dull trading as the banks are no longer in the market," one trader said.

China's central bank, the People's Bank, in early June ordered state banks to stop trading state debt on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges and regional debt trading centres, and to move their trading to the local currency interbank market.
"Some institutions were seen borrowing in the seven-day contract on Friday to prepare for the Shenzhen new share issue on Monday," a second trader said.
Traders said they expected the repo rates to experience a technical rebound on Monday.
Contracts on the T-bill spot market in Shanghai ended mostly up on Friday on good market sentiment, but trading was dull ahead of the weekend, traders said.
But the most actively traded 10-year bond that matures in June 2006 closed unchanged at 112.18 yuan.
Combined volume of the eight-contract market fell to 524,958 lots from 807,370 million lots.
Traders said an upward trend on the spot market, supported by high yields of existing contracts helped boost sentiment. The contracts now have an average yield of more than 10 percent.
Traders said they believed prices would continue to rise slightly the next week.
